questions.topic: Momentum and Impulse - Tennis Racket
questions.q: A tennis player receives a ball of mass $m = 60\text{ g}$, traveling horizontally at a speed of $50\text{ m/s}$, and hits it back with the racket sending it in the opposite direction at a speed of $40\text{ m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse transferred to the ball?
questions.hint: Impulse is equal to the change in momentum $I = \Delta q = m(v_f - v_i)$. Remember that the two velocities have opposite directions.
explanations: Correct! Converting mass to kilograms ($m = 0.06\text{ kg}$) and taking into account the opposite direction of the final velocity ($v_i = -50\text{ m/s}$ and $v_f = +40\text{ m/s}$), the impulse is $I = \Delta q = m(v_f - v_i) = 0.06 \cdot (40 - (-50)) = 0.06 \cdot 90 = 5.4\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (equal to $5.4\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$).
Incorrect. $0.6\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ is obtained by subtracting the magnitudes of the velocities ($50 - 40 = 10\text{ m/s}$) instead of adding them due to the opposite directions.
Incorrect. $2.4\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ considers only the final momentum of the ball without calculating its change.
Incorrect. $5400\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ is obtained by leaving the mass expressed in grams instead of kilograms.

questions.topic: Momentum and Impulse - Rebound off a Wall
questions.q: A steel ball of $3\text{ kg}$ strikes a wall at a speed of $10\text{ m/s}$, making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the wall. The ball rebounds with the same speed and at the same angle. If the ball stays in contact with the wall for $0.2\text{ s}$, what is the magnitude of the average force exerted by the wall on the ball?
questions.hint: Calculate the change in momentum along the axis perpendicular to the wall $\Delta q_x = -2 m v \sin 60^\circ$ and divide it by the contact time \Delta t.
explanations: Correct! The velocity component perpendicular to the wall is $v_x = v \sin 60^\circ$. Since motion along $x$ reverses, the change in momentum is $\Delta q_x = -2 m v \sin 60^\circ = -2 \cdot 3 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.866 = -51.96\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$. The magnitude of the average force is $F_m = \frac{|\Delta q_x|}{\Delta t} = \frac{51.96}{0.2} \approx 260\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. $150\text{ N}$ is obtained by using $\cos 60^\circ$ instead of $\sin 60^\circ$ for the normal component to the wall.
Incorrect. $300\text{ N}$ assumes a perpendicular collision with the wall, ignoring the $60^\circ$ inclination.
Incorrect. $130\text{ N}$ is obtained by forgetting the factor of $2$ due to the velocity direction reversal.

questions.topic: Inelastic Collisions - Final Velocity After Collision
questions.q: A car of mass $M_1 = 1800\text{ kg}$ stopped at a traffic light is rear-ended by a second car of mass $M_2 = 900\text{ kg}$ traveling at a speed $v_i = 20.0\text{ m/s}$. Assuming the two cars stick together and move as one, what is their speed immediately after the collision?
questions.hint: Apply conservation of momentum for a completely inelastic collision: $(M_1 + M_2) v_f = M_2 v_i$.
explanations: Correct! By conservation of momentum $q_i = q_f \implies M_2 v_i = (M_1 + M_2) v_f$. Therefore $v_f = \frac{M_2 v_i}{M_1 + M_2} = \frac{900 \cdot 20}{1800 + 900} = \frac{18000}{2700} \approx 6.67\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $10.00\text{ m/s}$ would only be obtained if the two cars had the same mass.
Incorrect. $13.33\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by mistakenly inverting the ratio of masses in the equation.
Incorrect. Calculation error in the sum of masses in the denominator.

questions.topic: Inelastic Collisions - Final Kinetic Energy
questions.q: A car $M_2 = 900\text{ kg}$ at $20.0\text{ m/s}$ rear-ends a stationary car $M_1 = 1800\text{ kg}$, becoming entangled with it. Knowing that after the collision their common speed is $6.67\text{ m/s}$, what is the remaining total kinetic energy of the system immediately after the collision?
questions.hint: Calculate the kinetic energy of the combined system of mass $M_1 + M_2 = 2700\text{ kg}$ at speed $v_f = 6.67\text{ m/s}$: $K_f = \frac{1}{2} (M_1 + M_2) v_f^2$.
explanations: Correct! The total mass of the system after the collision is $M_1 + M_2 = 2700\text{ kg}$. The final kinetic energy is $K_f = \frac{1}{2} (M_1 + M_2) v_f^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2700 \cdot (6.67)^2 \approx 60060\text{ J} \approx 60\text{ kJ}$.
Incorrect. $180000\text{ J}$ is the *initial* kinetic energy of the system $K_i = \frac{1}{2} M_2 v_i^2$ before the collision.
Incorrect. $119940\text{ J}$ corresponds to the kinetic energy *dissipated* during the inelastic collision ($K_i - K_f$).
Incorrect. $30030\text{ J}$ would be obtained by considering only the first car and ignoring the mass of the second.

questions.topic: Two-Dimensional Elastic Collisions - Final Velocity
questions.q: A billiard ball traveling at $v_i = 5\text{ m/s}$ hits a second ball of equal mass at rest, and continues with a speed $v_1 = 4.33\text{ m/s}$ angled at $30^\circ$ relative to the incoming direction. Assuming an elastic collision, what is the speed $v_2$ of the second ball immediately after the collision?
questions.hint: In an elastic collision between equal masses, conservation of kinetic energy holds: $v_i^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2 \implies v_2 = \sqrt{v_i^2 - v_1^2}$.
explanations: Correct! Since the masses are identical and the collision is elastic, the simplified kinetic energy equation is $v_i^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2 \implies v_2 = \sqrt{v_i^2 - v_1^2} = \sqrt{5^2 - 4.33^2} = \sqrt{25 - 18.75} = \sqrt{6.25} = 2.50\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $0.67\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by directly subtracting the speed magnitudes ($5 - 4.33$) instead of working with their squares.
Incorrect. Error in calculating the difference of squared velocities under the square root.
Incorrect. $1.25\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by mistakenly halving the correct speed value.

questions.topic: Two-Dimensional Elastic Collisions - Deflection Angle
questions.q: Another billiard ball of equal mass deflects with $v_1 = 4.33\text{ m/s}$ at $30^\circ$ after the elastic collision. Knowing that the second ball moves at $v_2 = 2.50\text{ m/s}$, what is the angle of inclination $\theta$ of the trajectory of the second ball relative to the initial direction?
questions.hint: Use conservation of momentum along the axis perpendicular to the initial direction: $0 = m v_1 \sin 30^\circ + m v_2 \sin \theta$.
explanations: Correct! By conservation of momentum along the vertical $y$-axis: $0 = m v_1 \sin 30^\circ + m v_2 \sin \theta \implies \sin \theta = -\frac{v_1 \sin 30^\circ}{v_2} = -\frac{4.33 \cdot 0.5}{2.5} = -0.866$. It follows that $|\theta| = \arcsin(0.866) = 60^\circ$ downward (the two final velocity vectors form an angle of $30^\circ + 60^\circ = 90^\circ$ between them).
Incorrect. $30^\circ$ is the deflection angle of the first ball.
Incorrect. $45^\circ$ would only be obtained if the two final speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$ were perfectly equal in magnitude.
Incorrect. $90^\circ$ is the total angle *between* the two outgoing directions of the balls, not the angle relative to the initial incoming direction.

questions.topic: Conservation of Momentum - Isolated Systems
questions.q: In an isolated system, total momentum is always conserved, in both elastic and inelastic collisions.
questions.hint: Consider whether the presence or absence of external forces is the sole factor determining the conservation of momentum.
explanations: Correct! Conservation of momentum ($\vec{q}_{tot} = \text{constant}$) depends solely on the absence of net external forces and holds for any type of collision (elastic, inelastic, or completely inelastic).
Incorrect. Total momentum is always conserved in isolated systems, regardless of whether kinetic energy is conserved.

questions.topic: Inelastic Collisions - Conservation and Energy Loss
questions.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision between two bodies, total momentum is not conserved because the maximum possible amount of kinetic energy is lost.
questions.hint: Distinguish between conservation of momentum and conservation of kinetic energy.
explanations: Correct! This is false: momentum is always conserved if no external forces act. In a perfectly inelastic collision, the maximum possible amount of kinetic energy is lost (the bodies stick together), but the total momentum of the system remains constant.
Incorrect. Do not confuse kinetic energy dissipation with momentum, which is still conserved in the absence of external forces.

questions.topic: Impulse-Momentum Theorem - Definition
questions.q: The impulse of a constant force applied to a body for a time interval $\Delta t$ is equal to the change in momentum of the body.
questions.hint: Recall the formulation of the impulse-momentum theorem $\vec{I} = \vec{F} \Delta t = \Delta \vec{q}$.
explanations: Correct! The impulse-momentum theorem states that $\vec{I} = \vec{F} \Delta t = \Delta \vec{q}$, i.e., the impulse transferred to a body is equal to the change in its momentum.
Incorrect. This is precisely the mathematical and conceptual definition of the impulse-momentum theorem.

questions.topic: One-Dimensional Elastic Collisions - Equal Masses
questions.q: In a head-on elastic collision between two bodies of equal mass, one of which is initially at rest, the incident body comes to a complete stop, transferring all its velocity to the second body.
questions.hint: Solve the system of conservation of momentum and kinetic energy by setting $m_1 = m_2$ and $v_{2i} = 0$.
explanations: Correct! For two equal masses ($m_1 = m_2$) with the second initially at rest ($v_{2i} = 0$), conservation of momentum and kinetic energy leads to $v_{1f} = 0$ and $v_{2f} = v_{1i}$. The two masses swap velocities exactly.
Incorrect. In elastic collisions between identical masses (such as billiard balls), the first mass stops, transferring its state of motion entirely to the second.

questions.topic: Physical Quantities - Unit of Measurement for Impulse
questions.q: Impulse is a scalar quantity whose SI unit of measurement is the Joule (J).
questions.hint: Check whether impulse has a direction and verify its SI unit of measurement ($\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ or $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$).
explanations: Correct! This is false: impulse is a vector quantity (it has magnitude, direction, and sense) and its SI unit is $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ (or $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$), whereas the Joule is the unit of measurement for energy and work.
Incorrect. Impulse is a vector and is measured in Newton-seconds ($\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$), not in Joules.

questions.topic: Elastic Collisions - Conservation of Kinetic Energy
questions.q: A collision is defined as elastic if the total kinetic energy of the system before impact is equal to the total kinetic energy after impact.
questions.hint: Recall the theoretical definition that distinguishes an elastic collision from an inelastic one.
explanations: Correct! By definition, in an elastic collision there is no dissipation of mechanical energy as heat or permanent deformation, so $K_i = K_f$.
Incorrect. Conservation of total kinetic energy is the fundamental defining characteristic of an elastic collision.

questions.topic: Impact Dynamics - Average Force and Contact Time
questions.q: For a given change in momentum $\Delta q$, an increase in contact time $\Delta t$ decreases the average force of the impact.
questions.hint: Analyze the formula for average force $F_m = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t}$.
explanations: Correct! Since $F_m = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t}$, if the impact time $\Delta t$ increases, the average force decreases. This is the working principle behind safety devices such as airbags and helmets.
Incorrect. Since time is in the denominator of the average force formula, extending the impact time cushions the collision by reducing the force.

questions.topic: Center of Mass - Motion During Collisions
questions.q: In an isolated system of two bodies, the velocity of the center of mass changes drastically if the collision is inelastic.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between total momentum and center of mass velocity: $\vec{v}_{cm} = \frac{\vec{q}_{tot}}{M_{tot}}$.
explanations: Correct! This is false: since total momentum $\vec{q}_{tot}$ of an isolated system is always conserved, the velocity of the center of mass $\vec{v}_{cm} = \frac{\vec{q}_{tot}}{M_{tot}}$ also remains completely constant during any type of collision.
Incorrect. In the absence of external forces, the center of mass continues its uniform straight-line motion unchanged before, during, and after the impact.

questions.topic: Center of Mass - X-Component of Velocity
questions.q: A system consists of two point masses: $m_1 = 2\text{ kg}$ with velocity $v_1 = (2, -3)\text{ m/s}$ and $m_2 = 3\text{ kg}$ with velocity $v_2 = (1, 6)\text{ m/s}$. What is the $x$-component of the center of mass velocity ($v_{CM,x}$)?
questions.hint: Apply the mass-weighted average formula: $v_{CM,x} = \frac{m_1 v_{1,x} + m_2 v_{2,x}}{m_1 + m_2}$.
explanations: Correct! The $x$-component of the center of mass velocity is $v_{CM,x} = \frac{m_1 v_{1,x} + m_2 v_{2,x}}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{2 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 1}{2 + 3} = \frac{7}{5} = 1.4\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $2.0\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by calculating a simple arithmetic mean of the velocities $\frac{2+1}{2} = 1.5$ or considering only the mass of the first particle.
Incorrect. $1.0\text{ m/s}$ corresponds only to the $x$-component of the velocity of the second body.
Incorrect. Calculation error in the denominator by dividing by only one of the two masses.

questions.topic: Center of Mass - Y-Component of Velocity
questions.q: For the same system of two point masses ($m_1 = 2\text{ kg}$ with $v_{1,y} = -3\text{ m/s}$; $m_2 = 3\text{ kg}$ with $v_{2,y} = 6\text{ m/s}$), what is the $y$-component of the center of mass velocity ($v_{CM,y}$)?
questions.hint: Use $v_{CM,y} = \frac{m_1 v_{1,y} + m_2 v_{2,y}}{m_1 + m_2}$, paying attention to the negative sign of $v_{1,y}$.
explanations: Correct! The $y$-component of the center of mass velocity is $v_{CM,y} = \frac{m_1 v_{1,y} + m_2 v_{2,y}}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{2 \cdot (-3) + 3 \cdot 6}{2 + 3} = \frac{-6 + 18}{5} = \frac{12}{5} = 2.4\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $1.5\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by taking a simple average of the velocities without weighting by their respective masses.
Incorrect. $3.6\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by ignoring the negative sign of component $v_{1,y}$.
Incorrect. Error in the sign of the numerator in the algebraic addition of the components.

questions.topic: Total Momentum - X-Component
questions.q: A system of two point masses has a total mass $M = m_1 + m_2 = 5\text{ kg}$ and a center of mass velocity with $x$-component $v_{CM,x} = 1.4\text{ m/s}$. What is the $x$-component of the total momentum of the system ($q_x$)?
questions.hint: Use the theorem stating that total momentum is equal to the product of total mass and center of mass velocity: $q_x = (m_1 + m_2) v_{CM,x}$.
explanations: Correct! Total momentum along $x$ is $q_x = (m_1 + m_2) v_{CM,x} = (2 + 3) \cdot 1.4 = 5 \cdot 1.4 = 7\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.
Incorrect. $3.5\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ would be obtained by multiplying $v_{CM,x}$ only by mass $m_1 = 2\text{ kg}$ or by half the total mass.
Incorrect. $14\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ would be obtained by mistakenly doubling the momentum result.
Incorrect. $5\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ corresponds to the numerical value of the total mass of the system.

questions.topic: Total Momentum - Y-Component
questions.q: For the same system of total mass $M = 5\text{ kg}$ and center of mass velocity with $y$-component $v_{CM,y} = 2.4\text{ m/s}$, what is the $y$-component of the total momentum of the system ($q_y$)?
questions.hint: Use the relationship $q_y = (m_1 + m_2) v_{CM,y}$.
explanations: Correct! Total momentum along $y$ is $q_y = (m_1 + m_2) v_{CM,y} = (2 + 3) \cdot 2.4 = 5 \cdot 2.4 = 12\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.
Incorrect. $6\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ would be obtained by calculating only the momentum of the second particle along $y$ ($m_2 v_{2,y} = 3 \cdot 6 = 18$) and subtracting incorrect values.
Incorrect. $24\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ would be obtained by mistakenly doubling the result.
Incorrect. Error in the product of total system mass and center of mass velocity.

questions.topic: Torque - Symbolic Expression for Net Torque
questions.q: A cylinder is free to rotate around its central axis. A string wrapped around a drum of radius $R_1$ exerts a force $T_1$ tending to rotate it clockwise, while a second string wrapped around radius $R_2$ exerts a force $T_2$ tending to rotate it counterclockwise. What is the expression for the net torque $\tau_{net}$ using the convention that counterclockwise is positive?
questions.hint: Torque is given by the product of the lever arm and the force. Assign a positive sign to counterclockwise torque and a negative sign to clockwise torque.
explanations: Correct! Force $T_1$ produces a clockwise torque $\tau_1 = -R_1 T_1$, while force $T_2$ produces a counterclockwise torque $\tau_2 = +R_2 T_2$. Adding the torques algebraically yields $\tau_{net} = R_2 T_2 - R_1 T_1$.
Incorrect. This expression would mistakenly assume clockwise as positive and counterclockwise as negative.
Incorrect. The two forces tend to rotate the cylinder in opposite directions, so their torques subtract rather than add.
Incorrect. Lever arms act separately on each applied force, not on the sum of the forces.

questions.topic: Torque - Calculation of Net Torque
questions.q: Considering the values $T_1 = 5.0\text{ N}$, $R_1 = 1.0\text{ m}$, $T_2 = 6.0\text{ N}$, and $R_2 = 0.50\text{ m}$, what is the value of the net torque $\tau_{net}$ relative to the rotation axis?
questions.hint: Substitute the values into the equation $\tau_{net} = R_2 T_2 - R_1 T_1$.
explanations: Correct! Substituting the data: $\tau_{net} = (6.0\text{ N} \cdot 0.50\text{ m}) - (5.0\text{ N} \cdot 1.0\text{ m}) = 3.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m} - 5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m} = -2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
Incorrect. $+2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ is obtained by reversing the signs of individual torques.
Incorrect. $-8.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ would be obtained by adding the magnitudes of the two torques instead of subtracting them.
Incorrect. $+3.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ is only the torque due to force $T_2$ without subtracting the torque due to $T_1$.

questions.topic: Rotational Dynamics - Direction of Cylinder Rotation
questions.q: A cylinder initially at rest is subjected to a net torque $\tau_{net} = -2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Knowing that the convention adopted defines clockwise torques as negative, in which direction will the cylinder rotate?
questions.hint: A negative net torque indicates that the prevailing torque pushes clockwise.
options: It will remain stationary in rotational equilibrium
It will start translating along the $z$-axis
explanations: Correct! Since the net torque is negative (meaning torque $\tau_1 = -5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ produced by the first force prevails), the cylinder will accelerate, rotating clockwise.
Incorrect. Counterclockwise rotation would require a positive net torque ($\tau_{net} > 0$).
Incorrect. To remain stationary or in rotational equilibrium, the net torque would have to be exactly zero ($\tau_{net} = 0$).
Incorrect. A torque along the rotation axis causes rotation around that axis, not translation.

questions.topic: Conservation of Angular Momentum - Validity Condition
questions.q: A mass $m$ rotates on a frictionless surface connected to a string passing through a hole in the center of the table. Why is angular momentum of the mass conserved while the string is pulled downward?
questions.hint: Calculate the torque of the string's tension with respect to the center of rotation (hole).
options: Because the force exerted by the string is central and passes through the axis of rotation, so its lever arm is zero and the net torque is zero.
Because the velocity of the mass during motion remains constant in magnitude and direction.
Because no radial force acts on the mass while the string is shortened.
explanations: Correct! The string tension acts along the radial direction pointing toward the center (axis of rotation). Having a zero lever arm relative to the point of rotation implies zero torque ($\tau = 0$), guaranteeing the conservation of angular momentum ($L = I\omega = \text{constant}$).
Incorrect. Tangential speed does not remain constant: it increases as the radius decreases.
Incorrect. The radial force is present—it is precisely the tension that keeps the mass in a circular orbit and reduces its radius.

questions.topic: Conservation of Angular Momentum - Tangential Speed Formula
questions.q: Applying conservation of angular momentum $m r_1^2 \omega_1 = m r_2^2 \omega_2$ to a particle of mass $m$, what is the correct expression for the final tangential speed $v_2$ in terms of $v_1$, $r_1$, and $r_2$?
questions.hint: Recall the relationship between tangential speed and angular speed $v = r \omega$.
explanations: Correct! Substituting $\omega = \frac{v}{r}$ into the conservation law $m r_1^2 \omega_1 = m r_2^2 \omega_2$, we obtain $m r_1^2 \left(\frac{v_1}{r_1}\right) = m r_2^2 \left(\frac{v_2}{r_2}\right) \implies m r_1 v_1 = m r_2 v_2 \implies v_2 = v_1 \frac{r_1}{r_2}$.
Incorrect. This formula would indicate a decrease in speed as the radius decreases, the opposite of what happens.
Incorrect. $\frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2}$ is the ratio of angular speeds $\frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}$, not tangential speeds.
Incorrect. The dependence of tangential speed on radii is linear with the ratio $\frac{r_1}{r_2}$, without a square root.

questions.topic: Conservation of Angular Momentum - Final Speed Calculation
questions.q: A mass initially rotates with a tangential speed $v_1 = 2.4\text{ m/s}$ along a circle of radius $r_1 = 0.80\text{ m}$. By pulling the string, the radius is reduced to $r_2 = 0.48\text{ m}$. What is the value of the new tangential speed $v_2$?
questions.hint: Substitute the data into the relationship $v_2 = v_1 \frac{r_1}{r_2}$.
explanations: Correct! Calculating $v_2 = v_1 \frac{r_1}{r_2} = 2.4 \cdot \frac{0.80}{0.48} = 2.4 \cdot 1.667 = 4.0\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $1.44\text{ m/s}$ is obtained by multiplying by the inverse ratio $\frac{r_2}{r_1} = \frac{0.48}{0.80}$.
Incorrect. $6.67\text{ m/s}$ is obtained by mistakenly applying the ratio of squares $\frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2}$.
Incorrect. Calculation error in the fraction $\frac{0.80}{0.48}$.
Incorrect. Value inconsistent with the principle of conservation of angular momentum.

questions.topic: Rotational Dynamics - Change in Angular Speed
questions.q: When the radius of rotation is reduced from $r_1 = 0.80\text{ m}$ to $r_2 = 0.48\text{ m}$, by what factor does the angular speed $\omega$ of the mass increase?
questions.hint: Calculate the ratio $\frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1} = \left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2$.
options: Increases by a factor of $\approx 2.78$ (equal to $\frac{25}{9}$)
Increases by a factor of $1.67$ (equal to $\frac{5}{3}$)
explanations: Correct! From the conservation of angular momentum $I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2 \implies m r_1^2 \omega_1 = m r_2^2 \omega_2$, we get $\frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1} = \frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2} = \left(\frac{0.80}{0.48}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{25}{9} \approx 2.78$.
Incorrect. $1.67$ is the factor of increase for *tangential* speed $v$, not angular speed $\omega$.
Incorrect. Angular speed increases as the radius decreases, it does not decrease.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - Effect of Internal Forces
questions.q: Internal forces acting between particles in a multi-body system cannot alter the total momentum of the system itself.
questions.hint: Consider Newton's Third Law of Motion (action and reaction) applied to pairs of internal forces.
explanations: Correct! By Newton's third law, internal forces act in equal and opposite pairs. Their vector sum is always zero, so internal forces cannot change the total momentum of the system.
Incorrect. Internal forces can alter the motion of individual particles, but their vector sum is zero and does not change total momentum.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - First Equation of Motion
questions.q: The center of mass of a multi-body system moves as if all the mass of the system were concentrated there and only the net external force acted upon it.
questions.hint: Recall the fundamental law for center of mass motion: $\vec{F}_{ext,tot} = M_{tot} \vec{a}_{CM}$.
explanations: Correct! This is the center of mass motion theorem: $\vec{F}_{ext,tot} = M_{tot} \vec{a}_{CM}$. The overall motion of the center of mass depends solely on external forces applied to the system.
Incorrect. It is a fundamental law of system dynamics for point masses.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - Work Done by Internal Forces
questions.q: The total work done by internal forces in a system of point masses is always zero, regardless of whether the system is rigid or deformable.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the work of internal forces when the relative distance between two points in the system changes (e.g., an explosion or a stretching spring).
explanations: Correct! This is false: the work done by internal forces is zero only for rigid bodies (where relative distances do not change). For deformable or non-rigid systems (such as a spring or an explosive charge), internal work can be non-zero and convert internal energy into kinetic energy.
Incorrect. If relative distances between particles change, the relative displacement makes the work of internal forces non-zero.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - König's Theorem for Kinetic Energy
questions.q: The total kinetic energy of a multi-body system is always equal solely to the kinetic energy associated with the motion of the center of mass.
questions.hint: Recall König's theorem: $K_{tot} = K_{CM} + K'$.
explanations: Incorrect. Total kinetic energy also includes energy from rotation or relative motion around the center of mass.

Correct! This is false: by König's theorem, total kinetic energy is the sum of the kinetic energy of the center of mass ($K_{CM} = \frac{1}{2} M v_{CM}^2$) and the kinetic energy of the particles relative to the center of mass ($K'$). The contribution $K'$ cannot be ignored.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - Acceleration of Individual Particles in Isolated Systems
questions.q: In an isolated multi-body system, the acceleration of each individual particle in the system must necessarily be zero.
questions.hint: Distinguish between the acceleration of the center of mass and the accelerations of individual particles caused by internal forces.
explanations: Correct! This is false: in an isolated system, the net external force is zero, so it is the acceleration *of the center of mass* that is zero. However, individual particles can accelerate due to internal forces exchanged between them.
Incorrect. Particles can interact internally (e.g., gravitational or electrical attraction) and thus accelerate, while maintaining a constant velocity of the center of mass.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - Conservation of Total Angular Momentum
questions.q: If the sum of torques from external forces relative to a fixed point is zero, the total angular momentum of the multi-body system is conserved.
questions.hint: Recall the second rotational equation of system dynamics: $\frac{d\vec{L}_{tot}}{dt} = \vec{\tau}_{ext,tot}$.
explanations: Correct! By the rotational equation of motion $\frac{d\vec{L}_{tot}}{dt} = \vec{\tau}_{ext,tot}$. If the net external torque is zero ($\vec{\tau}_{ext,tot} = 0$), total angular momentum $\vec{L}_{tot}$ remains constant over time.
Incorrect. It is the fundamental law of conservation of angular momentum for a multi-body system.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - Geometric Position of the Center of Mass
questions.q: The center of mass of a continuous or discrete system of bodies must necessarily lie within the material composing one of the bodies in the system.
questions.hint: Think about the position of the center of mass of a ring or a system formed by the Earth and the Moon.
explanations: Correct! This is false: the center of mass is a geometric point and can be located in empty space outside the bodies (for example, at the center of a ring or at a point in space between the Earth and the Moon).
Incorrect. The position of the center of mass depends on the average mass distribution and can be located in regions devoid of matter.

questions.topic: Multi-Body Systems - Momentum in the Center of Mass Frame
questions.q: The total momentum of a system of bodies, as measured by an observer in the center of mass frame of reference, is always equal to zero.
questions.hint: Consider what the velocity of the center of mass is as seen from the center of mass itself.
explanations: Correct! In the center of mass frame of reference (zero-momentum frame), the velocity of the center of mass is by definition zero ($v'_{CM} = 0$), and consequently the total momentum $\vec{q}'_{tot} = M_{tot} \vec{v}'_{CM} = 0$.
Incorrect. By definition of the center of mass frame, the vector sum of momenta relative to it is always zero.
